text.title: clean-architecture — Worked Examples
text.summary: Project folder layout, then one bounded context walked through the four layers in Python. Domain: User entity, Email value object, UserRepository abstract interface, domain events — all without framework imports. Application: CreateUserUseCase, GetUserUseCase, UnitOfWork interface, and UserDTO — orchestrating domain entities without ORM or HTTP. Infrastructure: SQLAlchemyUserRepository implementing the domain interface, SQLAlchemyUnitOfWork, and ORM model mapping. Closes with the two critical violations in code.

example.title: Four layer folders
example.code: src/ ├── domain/ # Entities layer │ ├── entities/ │ ├── value_objects/ │ ├── events/ │ ├── exceptions/ │ └── interfaces/ # Repository + service interfaces ├── application/ # Use cases layer │ ├── use_cases/ │ ├── interfaces/ # UnitOfWork, EventPublisher │ └── dto/ ├── infrastructure/ # Frameworks layer │ ├── persistence/ # Repository implementations, ORM models │ └── services/ # Email, payment, external APIs └── presentation/ # Interface adapters ├── api/ # Controllers, schemas, middleware └── cli/ # CLI commands
example.note: One folder per layer (r3-r6); the import-linter contract in `templates/import-linter.ini` pins the inward-only direction (r1, r2).

example.title: Entity: User
example.note: No ORM imports. No FastAPI imports. Testable with plain Python.

example.title: Value Object: Email
example.note: Frozen dataclass: validation and normalisation happen once, at construction.

example.title: Repository Interface
Use Case: CreateUser
example.note: No HTTP, no ORM, no framework imports. Accepts repository interface; works with any implementation. Testable with in-memory fakes.

example.title: UserDTO
example.note: Output DTO flattens the value object; presentation never touches the entity.

example.title: UnitOfWork Interface
Repository Implementation
example.note: _to_entity and _to_model perform the translation. The domain entity never imports UserModel. UserModel never enters the domain or application layers.

example.title: SQLAlchemy Unit of Work
example.code:
class SQLAlchemyUnitOfWork(UnitOfWork): def __init__(self, session: AsyncSession): self._session = session
async def __aenter__(self): return self
async def __aexit__(self, exc_type, exc_val, exc_tb): if exc_type: await self.rollback()
async def commit(self) -> None: await self._session.commit()
async def rollback(self) -> None: await self._session.rollback()
example.note: Implements the application-layer interface; the session type never leaks inward.

example.title: Domain logic in controller
example.code: @router.post("/users") async def create_user(request: CreateUserRequest, session=Depends(get_session)): if await session.execute(select(User).where(User.email == request.email)).scalar(): raise HTTPException(400, "Email exists") user = User(name=request.name, email=request.email) session.add(user) await session.commit() return user
example.note: fm-controller-business-logic: the uniqueness rule and entity construction live in the route.

example.title: Controller delegates to the use case
example.note: Thin glue: translate request to Input DTO, call one use case, translate Output DTO to response (r5).

example.title: Framework coupling in domain
example.note: fm-orm-in-entity: the entity is a persistence model.

example.title: Pure Python entity
example.code: @dataclass class User: # Pure Python, no framework imports email: Email name: str id: UUID = field(default_factory=uuid4) # ORM model lives in infrastructure/persistence/orm/models.py — separate class
example.note: Entity and ORM model are two classes in two layers; the repository maps between them (r3, r6).
